prompt.context: You are a consultant hired by a credit card company to analyze the better way to increase profitability on an individual account basis.
prompt.question: How would you analyze and improve profitability on a per-account basis for this credit card company?

clarifying_info.q: Are we focused on a specific customer segment or all accounts?
clarifying_info.a: All accounts — analyze profitability on an individual account basis across the full customer base.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any constraints on which levers we can use (e.g., pricing, marketing)?
clarifying_info.a: No constraints specified; consider both revenue and cost levers.

clarifying_info.q: How do our operations costs compare to the industry?
clarifying_info.a: Operations costs are currently in line with industry benchmarks.

framework: Define the per-account profit structure: Revenue minus Variable Costs (exclude fixed/advertising costs as they are independent of per-account profitability)
Revenue components: interest charged on outstanding balance (APR), annual fees, balance statement advertising revenue, late fees
Variable cost components: opportunity cost of capital (passive rate), operations costs (monthly statements), non-recoverable credits weighted by probability of permanent loss
Segment the customer base into profit-driver types to identify which customers to attract, retain, or shed
Identify levers on both the revenue side and the cost side to improve the per-account mix

questions.prompt: Walk through the per-account profit structure for a credit card company.
questions.guidance: Candidate should decompose Profit = Revenue - Variable Costs. Revenue: APR on outstanding balance, annual fees, balance-statement ad revenue, late fees. Variable Costs: cost of capital (passive rate), monthly statement operations, expected loss from non-recoverable credits (non-recoverable credit amount * probability of permanent loss). Fixed and advertising costs are excluded because they do not vary at the individual account level.

questions.prompt: You have talked about the composition of the credit card client pool. Go more deeply into that and explain how client type affects profitability.
questions.guidance: Three client types: (A) Clients who spend in line with income and pay in full every month — least profitable because the rate-differential profit source is lost. (B) Clients with expected future income growth who spend above current means — carry a significant outstanding balance and are highly profitable. (C) Clients who default, spending above their means with growing probability of non-recovery — the costliest segment.

questions.prompt: Draw or describe what a chart of account profitability (Y-axis) ranked from least to most profitable (X-axis) would look like given these three customer types.
questions.guidance: The curve is not monotonically increasing end-to-end. C-type accounts (defaulters) sit at the far left in deeply negative territory. A-type accounts (full-payers) cluster near zero or slightly positive. B-type accounts (revolvers with income growth) are the most profitable and sit at the far right. The shape: starts negative (C types), rises through near-zero (A types), then rises steeply into positive territory (B types).

questions.prompt: What actions would you recommend to improve the customer base mix?
questions.guidance: Attract more B-type customers: targeted marketing at students, people who just received a job offer, new parents — segments with high future-income-growth probability. Lower APR if market elasticity is high, to attract high-balance revolvers (B types) who would benefit from a lower rate. Charge a higher annual fee to deter A-type full-payers for whom the card has low value but raise the threshold for B types who benefit from revolving. Cleanse C-type customers from the portfolio by increasing late fees to incentivize on-time minimum payments and reduce default risk.

recommendation: Focus on attracting B-type customers (future income growth, high outstanding balance) through targeted marketing at students, new hires, and new parents, combined with a lower APR to capture high-balance revolvers if demand elasticity supports it
Raise the annual fee to filter out low-value A-type full-payers while remaining attractive to profitable B-type revolvers
Reduce C-type exposure by increasing late fees to pressure timely payments and shrink the non-recoverable credit pool
Operations costs are already at industry benchmarks so cost reduction focus should be on credit losses rather than operational efficiency
risks: Lowering APR may reduce per-account interest margin if elasticity assumptions are wrong
Higher annual fees may also drive away some B-type customers who are fee-sensitive
Aggressive late fees could push C-type clients to default faster rather than catch up on payments
next_steps: Quantify elasticity of demand for APR changes across customer segments
Model the net-profitability impact of annual fee increase versus lost A-type and potential B-type attrition
Pilot targeted marketing campaigns at high-income-growth demographic segments and measure acquisition cost vs. lifetime value
